story_text.value:
Hello. I built a blogging platform on my own over two years.

I like running my blog, but I couldn't find a blogging platform I really liked.

First. I thought a blog had to be really lightweight. Fortunately, after a lot of effort, I was able to achieve satisfactory results. (99 to 100 score)

Here is a sample blog: https://bloffy.bloffy.blog/en

You can check it with PageSpeed Insights: https://pagespeed.web.dev/analysis?url=https://bloffy.bloffy...

SEO score of the sample blog is low because I blocked it from search engine indexing (noindex).

Second. I think bloggers should have control over their own blog. The blogging platforms I used had several problems.

Unnecessary JavaScript chunks. Ads that the platform inserted into my blog, not my own ads. Cannot manage multiple blogs. An editor that makes it hard to write semantic markup. Limited customization options. I was dissatisfied with the difficulty of placing my own ads.

And to solve this, I spent quite a long time researching and developing it on my own, and finally created it. I'm glad to share this launch with HN. I would appreciate any criticism, feedback, and interest.

story_text.value:
ZeGrapher is a free an open-source math plotter, first release in 2011 (I thought there were no such app on Linux at the time), that I kept sporadically updating ever since. Last version was 6 years ago but a lot of work went into it.

v4 is a near complete rewrite to a modern interface and approach, inspired by desmos.

Interesting differenciating features:

- Computing and plotting recursive sequences - svg and pdf export at the physical size you see or set on your screen, in centimeters - "schrodinger" constants: define constants that take many values at once, any expression that depends on it is plotted for each value, with a user set color gradient. - an interesting graphical way to deal with CSVs and can handle large ones (millions of lines)

The rest on the website !

I want it to be able to make graphs that can be used in research articles, not quite there yet. I want math formatted (like katex) titles and legends at least.

Already found stuff to fix on this rc, feedback welcome!

story_text.value:
embodsi is a generative AI MMO experience that runs in the browser. It allows people to communicate (text, audio, video, avatar emotes and movement) and collaboratively build 3D spaces and games via LLMs connected to harnesses and sandboxes for object modeling, space layout, game logic, and driving persistent avatars with shared context and memory.

It’s different from existing 3D social apps (AFAIK) because it enables people to build multiplayer virtual worlds, games, and characters with generative AI right from their browser (desktop, mobile, or VR), in nearly infinitely-extendable recursively tiled interconnected spaces, while allowing people to interact in a public commons or easily create a private channel to enjoy the same spaces with their chosen friends and community.

The brief backstory is I was running my personal “pelican benchmark” [1] on GPT-6 Astra, which when I ran on Gemini 3 Pro last November couldn’t even put heads on 3D models the right side up [2], and was astounded by the initial results. I gained inspiration for an art project and social experiment that was going to have nine interconnected, benevolent virtual worlds that people could explore and hang out in with AI characters, but by the time Opus 5.5 was released I was gaining so much momentum and having so many ideas and so much fun building I just kept building more and more with the constraint of minimizing MVP scope lifted by agentic coding. I let the project become an ever-evolving wishlist of capabilities for a more interesting social environment as I became increasingly fascinated with the prospect of embodying creative machine intelligence in 3D space with people, realizing that rather than just limiting to building the spaces and characters I imagined I might enable people to co-create endless spaces and characters in a shared world.

There’s so much to do still but I’m sharing now even if it feels a little too soon (this is the first public announcement of embodsi’s existence) because I think it’s better to build in the open so people might guide the development and help it evolve in a good direction as model capability improves at a jaw-dropping pace.

For people that have the budget to build I hope to see you in embodsi creating amazing things! And for everyone regardless of means (I’ve tried to keep as much free and accessible as financially feasible) I hope you meet amazing people, discover awesome spaces, and enjoy your time in embodsi :)

I’ll be around here and embodsi to answer any questions! Thanks for your feedback and critique.

- Laser

P.S. SI != AI — but an emergent property of many people and what we create cascading and recursively interacting [3]

[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50074156

[2] https://x.com/lasernite/status/1991021951301923107

[3] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaia_hypothesis

story_text.value:
This package is designed to solve two problems:

1. Frontier models like Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Astra 6.0 and Sol 6.1 all make errors and bugs that can be found by another model (even a much smaller model like Luna).

2. In what is supposed to be a long development run, for example against a plan, models will decide to stop before they are finished, when there is obviously more work to do, or to ask a question they already should know the answer to.

ReviewerAgent blocks git commits and sends them to another agent that reviews the staged files and either allows the commit or returns a list of issues to fix.

StopContinue evaluates every agent stop and determines if it still has work to do or if it is asking a question that it has the answer to already. In either of those cases, it prompts the agent to keep working and specifies next steps or answers to questions, based on the current plan document and chat history.

The system works for and is tested on Claude Code and Codex as the developer harness, and either of those or any other model, through Pi, as the reviewer.

I've developed it over the last 4 months or so and used it daily over that period.

Take a look if it sounds useful. It's been tested on MacOS and Linux (Ubuntu), and has agent assisted install, update, and removal scripts, for convenience.

Stats:

Over four months of daily use of the system while developing it (from late June til today), reviewerAgent (usually a GPT Luna model) gated 3,877 commits, running about 7,600 reviews in total, so about half of those commits were rejected at least once.

The coding agent (Fable or Opus) almost never disagreed with the reviewer's judgements: over the last month, for example, it pushed back on just 3 of 693 rejections.

Each rejection listed an average of two required fixes and most rejected commits were accepted after a second round (90% within five attempts).

Rejection rates increased with commit size: only 23% of code commits under 50 lines were sent back, but 72% of those over 1,000 lines were initially rejected.

Here's an example of a bug that it caught last month for me. More examples in the README:

The Fable 5.1 developer agent wrote a wrapper script that runs a set of R validation checks against a freshly loaded database and records whether each one passed. (One of two required fixes shown.)

REQUIRED FIXES (blocking)

  2.  docs/database-phase-loader/local-load/run_r_checks.sh:4-6 pipes each R check through
      tail without pipefail or explicit status handling, so a failed Rscript can still
      produce a zero exit status and be recorded as successful. Preserve and propagate each
      check's exit status.
In a shell pipeline the exit status is that of the last command, so `Rscript check.R | tail` reports `tail`'s success even when the check fails. The script prints the tail of the failing check's output, exits 0, and records a pass. A broken load would have been certified as validated.

title.value: Show HN: ReviewerAgent and StopContinue, for CC and Codex with Pi

story_text.value:
I got tired of patching Tree-sitter grammars while I was building linting tools, so much so that I ended up writing a custom parsing framework and a bunch of custom grammars for popular languages. I figured I wasn't alone and that others would be hitting the same problem, especially with all the slop code being produced out there these days. So, I'm happy to now offer commercial support for an ever-expanding library of Tree-sitter compatible Wasm grammars that are continuously updated and well-tested.

Shoot me an email at info@powderworks.dev and we can get you set up. If there are specific languages that you want to use, let me know and I'll get them supported ASAP.

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

I usually have a couple of threads running on Codex, but some time ago I realized I was opening X or Instagram and doomscrolling while the agents did the work. I went from regularly getting into a flow state while coding manually to almost the complete opposite. Basically speedrunning a shorter attention span.

A friend and I built LightScroll partly to help with this. It's a screen time app for iOS and macOS that lets you choose your limits and how strict they should be.

I'm aware there are 999 competing screen time apps, but none worked quite right for us. So now there are 1000 competing screen time apps :)

It can range from just a short pause before opening a distracting app or website to needing a code from someone you've invited as an accountability partner.

It's free to get started and most of our friends/family are having good results using the free version daily so far.

Is anyone else finding themselves struggling to stay focused while waiting for coding agents to yield? What has helped you?

story_text.value:
I got irritated by the maximalism and lack of aesthetics present in modern software when trying to find a nice solitaire.

A solitaire does not need a score, levels - and most of all it does not need to download anything, have user log in or do anything else except maintain game state.

So since software comes automatically nowadays, I decided as a weekend project to create the last solitaire I'll ever need.

The application is built on Rust so I can compile it to native. But it runs just as well as web app!

I geeked out completely on design (it may look like "default" but that's the point) to create as non-intruding yet aesthetically pleasing experience as I could.

I might have accidentally put in a complete card design system with a content pipeline (maybe I'll do default blackjack next) - but as a player you only see the one pack of cards.

Anyway, hope someone here appreciates the minimalistic aesthetics.

The game state is saved in the url so if you want to save a nice game you can do it by copypasting the link.

The game engine is versioned so if I ever change the engine or state schema there will be support for the current version as well.

There _is_ a novelty.

If you click the "teach" button it shows all the available free moves as arrows.

Hope this is fun for someone!

story_text.value:
Hi all,

I had a hypothesis that YC companies sell to other YC companies. Many times to their own batch, other times to older YC companies. One of my YC friends told me that when they approached a big, well-known company for a potential pilot, the director of engineering there was a YC alum. He said "yeah, I understand" and gave them a pilot or LOI.

My theory is that most of the logos YC startups show on their landing pages will be other YC companies. They'll use that momentum at Demo Day to raise their seed round. What this also means is that sometimes, when I read Launch HNs or look at other YC products, I get the perception that they're very mature products (kudos to their design), and often that perception comes from the logos. So as someone looking to buy a YC product, I'm not sure if I'm being hustled or if they actually have a good customer base.

I'm not judging them. This is genuine curiosity, and also, this is what the YC advantage means. I set out to test my hypothesis by running my agents against YC's Summer 2026 batch: visit each landing page, look for customer logos, and check what percent of those are YC companies.

What do I get out of this? Probably nothing :p Just curious.

Here's a quick summary: - My hypothesis that most logos will be other YC companies is wrong. - In certain sub segments like horizontal AI tools, I did see that ~40% logos are YC companies.
